Uses physics-based energy indicators to structure input space, architectural constraints to limit admissible solutions, and hybrid loss formulations to enforce governing relations. Employs disjoint inference with decoupled surrogate models for impact velocity and mass, then computes impact energy via kinetic energy consistency.

Result: Mean absolute percentage errors below 8% for inferred impact velocity and impactor mass, below 10% for impact energy. Stable performance under reduced data availability and increased measurement noise. Generalizes to out-of-distribution cases across pristine and damaged regimes when damaged responses are included in training.

Conclusion: Systematic integration of physics-informed biases enables reliable, physically consistent, and data-efficient impact identification, demonstrating strong potential for practical monitoring systems.

Abstract: This paper introduces a novel physics-informed impact identification (Phy-ID) framework. The proposed method integrates observational, inductive, and learning biases to combine physical knowledge with data-driven inference in a unified modelling strategy, achieving physically consistent and numerically stable impact identification. The physics-informed approach structures the input space using physics-based energy indicators, constrains admissible solutions via architectural design, and enforces governing relations via hybrid loss formulations. Together, these mechanisms limit non-physical solutions and stabilise inference under degraded measurement conditions. A disjoint inference formulation is used as a representative use case to demonstrate the framework capabilities, in which impact velocity and impactor mass are inferred through decoupled surrogate models, and impact energy is computed by enforcing kinetic energy consistency. Experimental evaluations show mean absolute percentage errors below 8% for inferred impact velocity and impactor mass and below 10% for impact energy. Additional analyses confirm stable performance under reduced data availability and increased measurement noise, as well as generalisation for out-of-distribution cases across pristine and damaged regimes when damaged responses are included in training. These results indicate that the systematic integration of physics-informed biases enables reliable, physically consistent, and data-efficient impact identification, highlighting the potential of the approach for practical monitoring systems.

</details>


### [370] [Optimistic Actor-Critic with Parametric Policies for Linear Markov Decision Processes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.28595)
*Max Qiushi Lin,Reza Asad,Kevin Tan,Haque Ishfaq,Csaba Szepesvari,Sharan Vaswani*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes optimistic actor-critic with log-linear policies and Langevin Monte Carlo Thompson sampling for linear MDPs, achieving state-of-the-art sample complexity with practical implementation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing actor-critic theoretical analyses have limitations: they either sidestep exploration with strong assumptions or analyze impractical methods with complicated modifications. Methods for linear MDPs often use NPG with implicit policies that are computationally expensive to sample from, making environment interactions inefficient.

Method: Focuses on finite-horizon linear MDPs and proposes an optimistic actor-critic framework using parametric log-linear policies. Introduces tractable logit-matching regression objective for the actor. For the critic, uses approximate Thompson sampling via Langevin Monte Carlo to obtain optimistic value estimates.

Result: Proves the algorithm achieves $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(ε^{-4})$ and $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(ε^{-2})$ sample complexity in on-policy and off-policy settings respectively, matching state-of-the-art theoretical results while being more aligned with practice.

Conclusion: The proposed optimistic actor-critic framework with log-linear policies and Langevin Monte Carlo Thompson sampling achieves optimal sample complexity while being computationally efficient and practical compared to existing theoretical methods.

Abstract: Although actor-critic methods have been successful in practice, their theoretical analyses have several limitations. Specifically, existing theoretical work either sidesteps the exploration problem by making strong assumptions or analyzes impractical methods with complicated algorithmic modifications. Moreover, the actor-critic methods analyzed for linear MDPs often employ natural policy gradient (NPG) and construct "implicit" policies without explicit parameterization. Such policies are computationally expensive to sample from, making the environment interactions inefficient. To that end, we focus on the finite-horizon linear MDPs and propose an optimistic actor-critic framework that uses parametric log-linear policies. In particular, we introduce a tractable \textit{logit-matching} regression objective for the actor. For the critic, we use approximate Thompson sampling via Langevin Monte Carlo to obtain optimistic value estimates. We prove that the resulting algorithm achieves $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(ε^{-4})$ and $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(ε^{-2})$ sample complexity in the on-policy and off-policy setting, respectively. Our results match prior theoretical works in achieving the state-of-the-art sample complexity, while our algorithm is more aligned with practice.

</details>


### [371] [Position: Explainable AI is Causality in Disguise](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.28597)
*Amir-Hossein Karimi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper argues that the fragmentation in Explainable AI stems from lacking causal grounding, not missing ground truth, and proposes causal models as the necessary foundation for XAI.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The XAI field suffers from fragmentation, conflicting metrics, failed sanity checks, and unresolved debates over robustness and fairness, with no consensus on achieving explainability. Many attribute this to the absence of ground truth for defining correct explanations.

Method: The paper reframes XAI queries about data, models, or decisions as causal inquiries and proves the necessity and sufficiency of causal models for XAI. It advocates for convergence around advanced concept and causal discovery approaches.

Result: The paper demonstrates that causal models provide the elusive ground truth needed for XAI, arguing that without causal grounding, XAI remains unmoored and fragmented.

Conclusion: The persistent discord in XAI arises from an existing but elusive ground truth - the causal model governing the relevant system. The community should converge around causal discovery to escape entrenched uncertainty and provide proper foundations for explainability.

Abstract: The demand for Explainable AI (XAI) has triggered an explosion of methods, producing a landscape so fragmented that we now rely on surveys of surveys. Yet, fundamental challenges persist: conflicting metrics, failed sanity checks, and unresolved debates over robustness and fairness. The only consensus on how to achieve explainability is a lack of one. This has led many to point to the absence of a ground truth for defining ``the'' correct explanation as the main culprit.
  This position paper posits that the persistent discord in XAI arises not from an absent ground truth but from a ground truth that exists, albeit as an elusive and challenging target: the causal model that governs the relevant system. By reframing XAI queries about data, models, or decisions as causal inquiries, we prove the necessity and sufficiency of causal models for XAI. We contend that without this causal grounding, XAI remains unmoored. Ultimately, we encourage the community to converge around advanced concept and causal discovery to escape this entrenched uncertainty.

</details>


### [372] [LACE: Loss-Adaptive Capacity Expansion for Continual Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.28611)
*Shivnath Tathe*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LACE is an online continual learning method that automatically expands model capacity when loss deviation indicates insufficient representation for new data, achieving precise domain boundary detection without labels or replay buffers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fixed representational capacity forces practitioners to guess appropriate model width before training without knowing how many distinct concepts the data contains, creating a fundamental constraint in continual learning.

Method: LACE monitors the model's own loss signal during training; when sustained loss deviation exceeds a threshold (indicating insufficient capacity for new data), it adds new dimensions to the projection layer and trains them jointly with existing parameters.

Result: LACE achieves 100% boundary precision with zero false positives, matches large fixed-capacity model accuracy while starting from fewer dimensions, and shows adapter dimensions are critical (3% accuracy drop when removed). Unsupervised domain separation in GPT-2 shows U-shaped separability curve across layers.

Conclusion: LACE provides a simple, label-free, buffer-free mechanism for adaptive capacity expansion in continual learning, suitable for resource-constrained on-device applications while maintaining performance and precise domain boundary detection.

Abstract: Fixed representational capacity is a fundamental constraint in continual learning: practitioners must guess an appropriate model width before training, without knowing how many distinct concepts the data contains. We propose LACE (Loss-Adaptive Capacity Expansion), a simple online mechanism that expands a model's representational capacity during training by monitoring its own loss signal. When sustained loss deviation exceeds a threshold - indicating that the current capacity is insufficient for newly encountered data - LACE adds new dimensions to the projection layer and trains them jointly with existing parameters. Across synthetic and real-data experiments, LACE triggers expansions exclusively at domain boundaries (100% boundary precision, zero false positives), matches the accuracy of a large fixed-capacity model while starting from a fraction of its dimensions, and produces adapter dimensions that are collectively critical to performance (3% accuracy drop when all adapters removed). We further demonstrate unsupervised domain separation in GPT-2 activations via layer-wise clustering, showing a U-shaped separability curve across layers that motivates adaptive capacity allocation in deep networks. LACE requires no labels, no replay buffers, and no external controllers, making it suitable for on-device continual learning under resource constraints.

</details>


### [373] [Information-Theoretic Limits of Safety Verification for Self-Improving Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.28650)
*Arsenios Scrivens*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper establishes fundamental limits on safety gates for AI self-modification, showing classifier-based approaches cannot simultaneously achieve bounded cumulative risk and unbounded beneficial modifications, while verification-based methods can escape this impossibility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To determine whether safety mechanisms can permit unbounded beneficial self-modification while maintaining bounded cumulative risk, formalizing the dual requirements of sum(delta_n) < ∞ (bounded risk) and sum(TPR_n) = ∞ (unbounded utility).

Method: Theoretical analysis using Holder's inequality and NP counting methods to prove impossibility theorems for classifier-based gates, establishing universal finite-horizon ceilings, and demonstrating verification escape via Lipschitz ball verifiers with formal bounds for pre-LayerNorm transformers under LoRA.

Result: Classification impossibility: For power-law risk schedules with p > 1, any classifier-based gate forces sum(TPR_n) < ∞, making unbounded utility impossible. Universal finite-horizon ceiling shows maximum classifier utility grows subpolynomially as exp(O(√(log N))). Verification escape: Lipschitz ball verifiers achieve delta = 0 with TPR > 0, validated on GPT-2 with d_LoRA = 147,456 achieving conditional delta = 0 and TPR = 0.352.

Conclusion: Classifier-based safety gates fundamentally cannot achieve both bounded cumulative risk and unbounded beneficial self-modification, while verification-based approaches can escape this impossibility, establishing a strict separation between the two paradigms for AI safety.

Abstract: Can a safety gate permit unbounded beneficial self-modification while maintaining bounded cumulative risk? We formalize this question through dual conditions -- requiring sum delta_n < infinity (bounded risk) and sum TPR_n = infinity (unbounded utility) -- and establish a theory of their (in)compatibility.
  Classification impossibility (Theorem 1): For power-law risk schedules delta_n = O(n^{-p}) with p > 1, any classifier-based gate under overlapping safe/unsafe distributions satisfies TPR_n <= C_alpha * delta_n^beta via Holder's inequality, forcing sum TPR_n < infinity. This impossibility is exponent-optimal (Theorem 3). A second independent proof via the NP counting method (Theorem 4) yields a 13% tighter bound without Holder's inequality.
  Universal finite-horizon ceiling (Theorem 5): For any summable risk schedule, the exact maximum achievable classifier utility is U*(N, B) = N * TPR_NP(B/N), growing as exp(O(sqrt(log N))) -- subpolynomial. At N = 10^6 with budget B = 1.0, a classifier extracts at most U* ~ 87 versus a verifier's ~500,000.
  Verification escape (Theorem 2): A Lipschitz ball verifier achieves delta = 0 with TPR > 0, escaping the impossibility. Formal Lipschitz bounds for pre-LayerNorm transformers under LoRA enable LLM-scale verification. The separation is strict. We validate on GPT-2 (d_LoRA = 147,456): conditional delta = 0 with TPR = 0.352. Comprehensive empirical validation is in the companion paper [D2].

</details>


### [374] [AMIGO: Agentic Multi-Image Grounding Oracle Benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.28662)
*Min Wang,Ata Mahjoubfar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AMIGO is a benchmark for evaluating agentic vision-language models on long-horizon hidden-target identification tasks through multi-turn questioning under uncertainty with protocol constraints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current evaluations focus on single-image, single-turn correctness, but agentic vision-language models increasingly act through extended interactions, requiring benchmarks that stress long-horizon reasoning, uncertainty management, and protocol compliance.

Method: AMIGO uses a hidden-target identification protocol where an oracle privately selects a target image from a gallery of visually similar images, and the model must recover it by asking a sequence of attribute-focused Yes/No/Unsure questions under strict protocol constraints that penalize invalid actions with Skip.

Result: The benchmark is instantiated with the "Guess My Preferred Dress" task and includes comprehensive metrics covering identification success, evidence verification, efficiency, protocol compliance, noise tolerance, and trajectory-level diagnostics.

Conclusion: AMIGO provides a rigorous benchmark for evaluating agentic vision-language models on long-horizon interactive tasks that require question selection under uncertainty, consistent constraint tracking, and fine-grained discrimination as evidence accumulates, with controlled oracle imperfections to probe robustness.

Abstract: Agentic vision-language models increasingly act through extended interactions, but most evaluations still focus on single-image, single-turn correctness. We introduce AMIGO (Agentic Multi-Image Grounding Oracle Benchmark), a long-horizon benchmark for hidden-target identification over galleries of visually similar images. In AMIGO, the oracle privately selects a target image, and the model must recover it by asking a sequence of attribute-focused Yes/No/Unsure questions under a strict protocol that penalizes invalid actions with Skip. This setting stresses (i) question selection under uncertainty, (ii) consistent constraint tracking across turns, and (iii) fine-grained discrimination as evidence accumulates. AMIGO also supports controlled oracle imperfections to probe robustness and verification behavior under inconsistent feedback. We instantiate AMIGO with Guess My Preferred Dress task and report metrics covering both outcomes and interaction quality, including identification success, evidence verification, efficiency, protocol compliance, noise tolerance, and trajectory-level diagnostics.

</details>


### [375] [FL-PBM: Pre-Training Backdoor Mitigation for Federated Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.28673)
*Osama Wehbi,Sarhad Arisdakessian,Omar Abdel Wahab,Azzam Mourad,Hadi Otrok,Jamal Bentahar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FL-PBM is a pre-training defense for federated learning that proactively filters poisoned data using benign trigger insertion, PCA feature extraction, GMM clustering, and targeted blurring to reduce backdoor attack success rates by up to 95% while maintaining clean accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Backdoor attacks pose significant threats to AI model integrity in critical applications like autonomous driving, healthcare, and finance. Detecting and mitigating these attacks is crucial throughout model lifecycle phases (pre-training, in-training, post-training), especially in federated learning environments where data is distributed across clients.

Method: FL-PBM employs a four-stage client-side defense: (1) Insert benign triggers into data to establish controlled baseline, (2) Apply PCA to extract discriminative features and assess data separability, (3) Perform GMM clustering to identify potentially malicious samples based on distribution in PCA-transformed space, (4) Apply targeted blurring technique to disrupt potential backdoor triggers.

Result: Experimental evaluations on image datasets show FL-PBM reduces attack success rates by up to 95% compared to baseline FedAvg and by 30-80% relative to state-of-the-art defenses (RDFL and LPSF). It maintains over 90% clean model accuracy in most experiments, achieving effective mitigation without performance degradation.

Conclusion: FL-PBM provides an effective pre-training defense mechanism for federated learning that proactively filters poisoned data on the client side, significantly reducing backdoor attack success while preserving model accuracy, offering better mitigation than existing state-of-the-art defenses.

Abstract: Backdoor attacks pose a significant threat to the integrity and reliability of Artificial Intelligence (AI) models, enabling adversaries to manipulate model behavior by injecting poisoned data with hidden triggers. These attacks can lead to severe consequences, especially in critical applications such as autonomous driving, healthcare, and finance. Detecting and mitigating backdoor attacks is crucial across the lifespan of model's phases, including pre-training, in-training, and post-training. In this paper, we propose Pre-Training Backdoor Mitigation for Federated Learning (FL-PBM), a novel defense mechanism that proactively filters poisoned data on the client side before model training in a federated learning (FL) environment. The approach consists of three stages: (1) inserting a benign trigger into the data to establish a controlled baseline, (2) applying Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to extract discriminative features and assess the separability of the data, (3) performing Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) clustering to identify potentially malicious data samples based on their distribution in the PCA-transformed space, and (4) applying a targeted blurring technique to disrupt potential backdoor triggers. Together, these steps ensure that suspicious data is detected early and sanitized effectively, thereby minimizing the influence of backdoor triggers on the global model. Experimental evaluations on image-based datasets demonstrate that FL-PBM reduces attack success rates by up to 95% compared to baseline federated learning (FedAvg) and by 30 to 80% relative to state-of-the-art defenses (RDFL and LPSF). At the same time, it maintains over 90% clean model accuracy in most experiments, achieving better mitigation without degrading model performance.

</details>


<div id='cs.IR'></div>

# cs.IR [[Back]](#toc)

### [376] [M-RAG: Making RAG Faster, Stronger, and More Efficient](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.26667)
*Sun Xu,Tongkai Xu,Baiheng Xie,Li Huang,Qiang Gao,Kunpeng Zhang*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: M-RAG proposes a chunk-free retrieval strategy using structured meta-markers instead of text chunks, improving efficiency and evidence quality in retrieval-augmented generation systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional RAG systems suffer from information fragmentation, retrieval noise, and reduced efficiency due to text chunking. While long-context LLMs can process full documents, they still struggle with relevance filtering, evidence prioritization, and isolating answer-bearing information.

Method: M-RAG extracts structured key-value decomposition meta-markers: lightweight, intent-aligned retrieval keys for similarity matching, and context-rich information values for generation. This decouples retrieval representation from generation, enabling efficient query-key matching without sacrificing expressive ability.

Result: M-RAG outperforms chunk-based RAG baselines on LongBench subtasks across varying token budgets, especially under low-resource settings. It retrieves more answer-friendly evidence with high efficiency and demonstrates scalability and robustness.

Conclusion: The chunk-free meta-marker approach effectively addresses limitations of traditional chunk-based RAG by decoupling retrieval and generation representations, offering a scalable and robust alternative that maintains efficiency while improving evidence quality.

Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has become a widely adopted paradigm for enhancing the reliability of large language models (LLMs). However, RAG systems are sensitive to retrieval strategies that rely on text chunking to construct retrieval units, which often introduce information fragmentation, retrieval noise, and reduced efficiency. Recent work has even questioned the necessity of RAG, arguing that long-context LLMs may eliminate multi-stage retrieval pipelines by directly processing full documents. Nevertheless, expanded context capacity alone does not resolve the challenges of relevance filtering, evidence prioritization, and isolating answer-bearing information. To this end, we proposed M-RAG, a novel Chunk-free retrieval strategy. Instead of retrieving coarse-grained textual chunks, M-RAG extracts structured, k-v decomposition meta-markers, with a lightweight, intent-aligned retrieval key for retrieval and a context-rich information value for generation. Under this setting, M-RAG enables efficient and stable query-key similarity matching without sacrificing expressive ability. Experimental results on the LongBench subtasks demonstrate that M-RAG outperforms chunk-based RAG baselines across varying token budgets, particularly under low-resource settings. Extensive analysis further reveals that M-RAG retrieves more answer-friendly evidence with high efficiency, validating the effectiveness of decoupling retrieval representation from generation and highlighting the proposed strategy as a scalable and robust alternative to existing chunk-based methods.

</details>


### [377] [Bridge-RAG: An Abstract Bridge Tree Based Retrieval Augmented Generation Algorithm With Cuckoo Filter](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.26668)
*Zihang Li,Wenjun Liu,Yikun Zong,Jiawen Tao,Siying Dai,Songcheng Ren,Zirui Liu,Yanbing Jiang,Tong Yang*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: Bridge-RAG is a novel retrieval-augmented generation framework that improves both accuracy and efficiency through abstract bridging, tree-structured organization, and optimized data structures including improved Cuckoo Filter and block linked lists.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current RAG frameworks face two main challenges: retrieval accuracy limitations and computational inefficiency. The paper aims to address both issues simultaneously to enhance LLM generation quality.

Method: Introduces abstract concepts to bridge query entities and document chunks for better semantic understanding. Organizes abstracts into a tree structure with multi-level retrieval strategy. Uses improved Cuckoo Filter for efficient entity location, and implements block linked list structure with entity temperature-based sorting for spatial and temporal locality optimization.

Result: Bridge-RAG achieves approximately 15.65% accuracy improvement and reduces retrieval time by 10x to 500x compared to other RAG frameworks in extensive experiments.

Conclusion: Bridge-RAG successfully addresses both accuracy and efficiency challenges in RAG systems through its novel bridging approach and optimized data structures, demonstrating significant performance improvements over existing frameworks.

Abstract: As an important paradigm for enhancing the generation quality of Large Language Models (LLMs), retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) faces the two challenges regarding retrieval accuracy and computational efficiency. This paper presents a novel RAG framework called Bridge-RAG. To overcome the accuracy challenge, we introduce the concept of abstract to bridge query entities and document chunks, providing robust semantic understanding. We organize the abstracts into a tree structure and design a multi-level retrieval strategy to ensure the inclusion of sufficient contextual information. To overcome the efficiency challenge, we introduce the improved Cuckoo Filter, an efficient data structure supporting rapid membership queries and updates, to accelerate entity location during the retrieval process. We design a block linked list structure and an entity temperature-based sorting mechanism to improve efficiency from the aspects of spatial and temporal locality. Extensive experiments show that Bridge-RAG achieves around 15.65% accuracy improvement and reduces 10x to 500x retrieval time compared to other RAG frameworks.

</details>


### [378] [ReCQR: Incorporating conversational query rewriting to improve Multimodal Image Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.26669)
*Yuan Hu,ZhiYu Cao,PeiFeng Li,QiaoMing Zhu*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: This paper introduces conversational query rewriting (CQR) for image retrieval, creates the ReCQR dataset with 7,000 multimodal dialogues, and shows CQR improves retrieval accuracy by rewriting ambiguous queries into clear, complete ones.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing image retrievers struggle with processing long texts and handling unclear user expressions in multimodal learning contexts, creating a need for better query understanding and processing.

Method: 1) Introduce conversational query rewriting (CQR) task that rewrites users' final queries using full dialogue histories; 2) Create ReCQR dataset using LLMs to generate rewritten candidates at scale, then apply LLM-as-Judge mechanism with manual review; 3) Benchmark SOTA multimodal models on ReCQR to assess image retrieval performance.

Result: Created ReCQR dataset with approximately 7,000 high-quality multimodal dialogues; Experimental results show CQR significantly enhances accuracy of traditional image retrieval models and provides new directions for modeling user queries in multimodal systems.

Conclusion: Conversational query rewriting effectively addresses limitations of existing image retrievers by transforming ambiguous queries into concise, semantically complete ones, offering a promising approach for improving multimodal retrieval systems.

Abstract: With the rise of multimodal learning, image retrieval plays a crucial role in connecting visual information with natural language queries. Existing image retrievers struggle with processing long texts and handling unclear user expressions. To address these issues, we introduce the conversational query rewriting (CQR) task into the image retrieval domain and construct a dedicated multi-turn dialogue query rewriting dataset. Built on full dialogue histories, CQR rewrites users' final queries into concise, semantically complete ones that are better suited for retrieval. Specifically, We first leverage Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate rewritten candidates at scale and employ an LLM-as-Judge mechanism combined with manual review to curate approximately 7,000 high-quality multimodal dialogues, forming the ReCQR dataset. Then We benchmark several SOTA multimodal models on the ReCQR dataset to assess their performance on image retrieval. Experimental results demonstrate that CQR not only significantly enhances the accuracy of traditional image retrieval models, but also provides new directions and insights for modeling user queries in multimodal systems.

</details>


### [379] [SRAG: RAG with Structured Data Improves Vector Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.26670)
*Shalin Shah,Srikanth Ryali,Ramasubbu Venkatesh*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: SRAG enhances traditional RAG by incorporating structured metadata (topics, sentiments, types, knowledge graph triples, semantic tags) into query and chunk representations, improving retrieval quality by 30% in QA systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional RAG relies solely on representational similarity between queries and chunks, which limits retrieval effectiveness. The performance depends heavily on numeric vector representations, suggesting a need for richer, structured information to improve grounding.

Method: Proposes Structured RAG (SRAG) that augments both queries and chunks with structured metadata including: topics, sentiments, query/chunk types (informational, quantitative), knowledge graph triples, and semantic tags. This enriched representation improves retrieval beyond simple vector similarity.

Result: Using GPT-5 as LLM-as-a-judge, SRAG improves answer scores in QA systems by 30% (p-value = 2e-13). Strongest improvements observed for comparative, analytical, and predictive questions. Enables broader, more diverse, episodic-style retrieval. Tail risk analysis shows SRAG achieves large gains frequently with minor losses.

Conclusion: Incorporating structured information into RAG representations significantly enhances retrieval quality, particularly for complex question types. The approach enables more effective information grounding for LLMs through richer semantic representations.

Abstract: Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) provides the necessary informational grounding to LLMs in the form of chunks retrieved from a vector database or through web search. RAG could also use knowledge graph triples as a means of providing factual information to an LLM. However, the retrieval is only based on representational similarity between a question and the contents. The performance of RAG depends on the numeric vector representations of the query and the chunks. To improve these representations, we propose Structured RAG (SRAG), which adds structured information to a query as well as the chunks in the form of topics, sentiments, query and chunk types (e.g., informational, quantitative), knowledge graph triples and semantic tags. Experiments indicate that this method significantly improves the retrieval process. Using GPT-5 as an LLM-as-a-judge, results show that the method improves the score given to answers in a question answering system by 30% (p-value = 2e-13) (with tighter bounds). The strongest improvement is in comparative, analytical and predictive questions. The results suggest that our method enables broader, more diverse, and episodic-style retrieval. Tail risk analysis shows that SRAG attains very large gains more often, with losses remaining minor in magnitude.

</details>


### [380] [LITTA: Late-Interaction and Test-Time Alignment for Visually-Grounded Multimodal Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.26683)
*Seonok Kim*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: LITTA improves multimodal document retrieval via query expansion without retraining, using LLM-generated query variants and reciprocal rank fusion to enhance evidence coverage across visually rich documents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Retrieving evidence from visually rich documents (textbooks, technical reports, manuals) is challenging due to long context, complex layouts, and weak lexical overlap between user questions and supporting pages.

Method: Query-expansion-centric framework: 1) Generate complementary query variants using LLM, 2) Retrieve candidate pages for each variant using frozen vision retriever with late-interaction scoring, 3) Aggregate candidates through reciprocal rank fusion to improve coverage and reduce sensitivity to phrasing.

Result: Significantly improves retrieval robustness across computer science, pharmaceuticals, and industrial manuals domains. Multi-query retrieval consistently improves top-k accuracy, recall, and MRR, with largest gains in domains with high visual/semantic variability. Accuracy-efficiency trade-off controllable by number of query variants.

Conclusion: Query expansion provides simple yet effective mechanism for improving visually grounded multimodal retrieval without retriever retraining, remaining compatible with existing multimodal embedding indices and practical for deployment under latency constraints.

Abstract: Retrieving relevant evidence from visually rich documents such as textbooks, technical reports, and manuals is challenging due to long context, complex layouts, and weak lexical overlap between user questions and supporting pages. We propose LITTA, a query-expansion-centric retrieval framework for evidence page retrieval that improves multimodal document retrieval without retriever retraining. Given a user query, LITTA generates complementary query variants using a large language model and retrieves candidate pages for each variant using a frozen vision retriever with late-interaction scoring. Candidates from expanded queries are then aggregated through reciprocal rank fusion to improve evidence coverage and reduce sensitivity to any single phrasing. This simple test-time strategy significantly improves retrieval robustness while remaining compatible with existing multimodal embedding indices. We evaluate LITTA on visually grounded document retrieval tasks across three domains: computer science, pharmaceuticals, and industrial manuals. Multi-query retrieval consistently improves top-k accuracy, recall, and MRR compared to single-query retrieval, with particularly large gains in domains with high visual and semantic variability. Moreover, the accuracy-efficiency trade-off is directly controllable by the number of query variants, making LITTA practical for deployment under latency constraints. These results demonstrate that query expansion provides a simple yet effective mechanism for improving visually grounded multimodal retrieval.

</details>


### [381] [EVNextTrade: Learning-to-Rank-Based Recommendation of Next Charging Nodes for EV-EV Energy Trading](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.26688)
*Md Mahfujur Rahmana,Alistair Barros,Raja Jurdak,Darshika Koggalahewa*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: This paper proposes a learning-to-rank framework to recommend optimal charging nodes for peer-to-peer EV energy trading, addressing uncertainty in mobility patterns and using probabilistic relevance refinement with gradient-boosted models on large-scale urban EV data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While prior EV-EV energy trading research focused on transaction management or isolated mobility prediction, there's a gap in identifying which charging nodes are more suitable for EV-EV trading in journey contexts. The problem of recommending optimal charging nodes for decentralized energy trading remains open.

Method: Formulates next charging nodes recommendation as a learning-to-rank problem using a supervised ranking framework on large-scale urban EV mobility data. Employs probabilistic relevance refinement to generate graded labels accounting for mobility uncertainty. Evaluates gradient-boosted learning-to-rank models (LightGBM, XGBoost, CatBoost) on EV journey records enriched with candidate charging nodes and multidimensional features including energy level, trading role, distance, charging speed, and temporal station popularity.

Result: LightGBM consistently achieves the strongest ranking performance across standard metrics (NDCG@k, Recall@k, MRR), with particularly strong early-ranking quality: highest NDCG@1 (0.9795) and MRR (0.9990). The uncertainty-aware learning-to-rank approach effectively recommends charging nodes for EV-EV energy trading.

Conclusion: The proposed framework demonstrates effectiveness of uncertainty-aware learning-to-rank for charging node recommendation, supporting improved coordination and matching in decentralized EV-EV energy trading systems by addressing mobility uncertainty and multiple viable charging options.

Abstract: Peer-to-peer energy trading among electric vehicles (EVs) has been increasingly studied as a promising solution for improving supply-side resilience under growing charging demand and constrained charging infrastructure. While prior studies on EV-EV energy trading and related EV research have largely focused on transaction management or isolated mobility prediction tasks, the problem of identifying which charging nodes are more suitable for EV-EV trading in journey contexts remains open. We address this gap by formulating next charging nodes recommendation as a learning-to-rank problem, where each EV decision event is associated with a set of candidate charging locations. We propose a supervised ranking framework applied to a large-scale urban EV mobility dataset comprising millions of journey records and multidimensional EV trading-related features, including EV energy level, trading role, distance to charging locations, charging speed, and temporal station popularity. To account for uncertainty arising from the mobility of both energy providers and consumers, as well as the presence of multiple viable charging nodes at a decision point, we employ probabilistic relevance refinement to generate graded labels for ranking. We evaluate gradient-boosted learning-to-rank models, including LightGBM, XGBoost, and CatBoost, on EV journey records enriched with candidate charging nodes. Experimental results show that LightGBM consistently achieves the strongest ranking performance across standard metrics, including NDCG@k, Recall@k, and MRR, with particularly strong early-ranking quality, reflected in the highest NDCG@1 (0.9795) and MRR (0.9990). These results highlight the effectiveness of uncertainty-aware learning-to-rank for charging node recommendation and support improved coordination and matching in decentralized EV-EV energy trading systems.

</details>


### [382] [Agentic AI for Human Resources: LLM-Driven Candidate Assessment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.26710)
*Kamer Ali Yuksel,Abdul Basit Anees,Ashraf Elneima,Sanjika Hewavitharana,Mohamed Al-Badrashiny,Hassan Sawaf*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: A modular LLM framework for automated candidate assessment using role-specific rubrics and multi-agent architecture, plus an LLM-Driven Active Listwise Tournament mechanism for principled candidate ranking.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address limitations of traditional ATS tools (keyword matching, shallow scoring) by creating a transparent, interpretable system that mirrors expert judgment in recruitment assessment and provides principled candidate ranking.

Method: 1) Modular framework integrating job descriptions, CVs, interview transcripts, and HR feedback with LLM-generated role-specific rubrics and multi-agent architecture for fine-grained evaluation. 2) LLM-Driven Active Listwise Tournament: LLM ranks small candidate subsets (mini-tournaments), aggregates permutations via Plackett-Luce model, and uses active-learning to select informative subsets for sample-efficient ranking.

Result: System generates structured evaluation reports, candidate comparisons, and ranked recommendations that are transparent, auditable, and suitable for real-world hiring workflows. Provides globally coherent rankings through the listwise tournament mechanism.

Conclusion: The framework offers a principled, interpretable methodology for large-scale candidate assessment and ranking in talent acquisition, adapting listwise LLM preference modeling from financial domains to recruitment contexts.

Abstract: In this work, we present a modular and interpretable framework that uses Large Language Models (LLMs) to automate candidate assessment in recruitment. The system integrates diverse sources, including job descriptions, CVs, interview transcripts, and HR feedback; to generate structured evaluation reports that mirror expert judgment. Unlike traditional ATS tools that rely on keyword matching or shallow scoring, our approach employs role-specific, LLM-generated rubrics and a multi-agent architecture to perform fine-grained, criteria-driven evaluations. The framework outputs detailed assessment reports, candidate comparisons, and ranked recommendations that are transparent, auditable, and suitable for real-world hiring workflows.
  Beyond rubric-based analysis, we introduce an LLM-Driven Active Listwise Tournament mechanism for candidate ranking. Instead of noisy pairwise comparisons or inconsistent independent scoring, the LLM ranks small candidate subsets (mini-tournaments), and these listwise permutations are aggregated using a Plackett-Luce model. An active-learning loop selects the most informative subsets, producing globally coherent and sample-efficient rankings. This adaptation of listwise LLM preference modeling (previously explored in financial asset ranking) provides a principled and highly interpretable methodology for large-scale candidate ranking in talent acquisition.

</details>


### [383] [GroupRAG: Cognitively Inspired Group-Aware Retrieval and Reasoning via Knowledge-Driven Problem Structuring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.26807)
*Xinyi Duan,Yuanrong Tang,Jiangtao Gong*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: GroupRAG improves language model performance by modeling problem structure through knowledge-driven keypoint grouping, enabling multi-start retrieval and reasoning instead of single inference chains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current approaches like RAG and CoT have limitations in real-world settings due to insufficient awareness of problem structure. Inspired by cognitive science showing human problem solving as search over structured problem spaces, the authors identify inadequate problem structure awareness as a key overlooked limitation.

Method: GroupRAG is a cognitively inspired, group-aware retrieval and reasoning framework based on knowledge-driven keypoint grouping. It identifies latent structural groups within problems and performs retrieval and reasoning from multiple conceptual starting points, enabling fine-grained interaction between retrieval and reasoning processes.

Result: Experiments on MedQA show that GroupRAG outperforms representative RAG- and CoT-based baselines.

Conclusion: Explicitly modeling problem structure, as inspired by human cognition, is a promising direction for robust retrieval-augmented reasoning.

Abstract: The performance of language models is commonly limited by insufficient knowledge and constrained reasoning. Prior approaches such as Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and Chain-of-Thought (CoT) address these issues by incorporating external knowledge or enforcing linear reasoning chains, but often degrade in real-world settings. Inspired by cognitive science, which characterizes human problem solving as search over structured problem spaces rather than single inference chains, we argue that inadequate awareness of problem structure is a key overlooked limitation. We propose GroupRAG, a cognitively inspired, group-aware retrieval and reasoning framework based on knowledge-driven keypoint grouping. GroupRAG identifies latent structural groups within a problem and performs retrieval and reasoning from multiple conceptual starting points, enabling fine-grained interaction between the two processes. Experiments on MedQA show that GroupRAG outperforms representative RAG- and CoT-based baselines. These results suggest that explicitly modeling problem structure, as inspired by human cognition, is a promising direction for robust retrieval-augmented reasoning.

</details>


### [384] [On the Accuracy Limits of Sequential Recommender Systems: An Entropy-Based Approach](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.27952)
*En Xu,Jingtao Ding,Yong Li*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: The paper proposes a training-free, entropy-based estimator for quantifying the intrinsic accuracy limits of sequential recommender systems, addressing limitations of existing predictability analyses and providing model-agnostic difficulty assessment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current sequential recommender systems show steady offline accuracy gains, but there's no reliable way to estimate the intrinsic accuracy ceiling imposed by data. Existing predictability analyses suffer from sensitivity to candidate-space specification and distortion from Fano-based scaling in low-predictability regimes, making principled difficulty assessment and headroom estimation challenging before costly model development.

Method: Develops an entropy-induced, training-free approach for quantifying accuracy limits in sequential recommendation. The method yields candidate-size-agnostic estimates by addressing limitations of existing approaches that combine entropy estimation with Fano's inequality inversion. The estimator tracks oracle-controlled difficulty and remains insensitive to candidate-set size.

Result: Experiments on synthetic generators and real-world benchmarks show the estimator: 1) tracks oracle-controlled difficulty more faithfully than baselines, 2) remains insensitive to candidate-set size, 3) achieves high rank consistency with best-achieved offline accuracy across state-of-the-art sequential recommenders (Spearman rho up to 0.914), 4) supports user-group diagnostics by stratifying users by novelty preference, long-tail exposure, and activity, revealing systematic predictability differences, and 5) guides training data selection where high-predictability users yield strong downstream performance under reduced data budgets.

Conclusion: The proposed estimator provides a practical reference for assessing attainable accuracy limits, supporting user-group diagnostics, and informing data-centric decisions in sequential recommendation. It enables principled difficulty assessment and headroom estimation before costly model development, addressing a critical gap in evaluating recommender system potential.

Abstract: Sequential recommender systems have achieved steady gains in offline accuracy, yet it remains unclear how close current models are to the intrinsic accuracy limit imposed by the data. A reliable, model-agnostic estimate of this ceiling would enable principled difficulty assessment and headroom estimation before costly model development. Existing predictability analyses typically combine entropy estimation with Fano's inequality inversion; however, in recommendation they are hindered by sensitivity to candidate-space specification and distortion from Fano-based scaling in low-predictability regimes. We develop an entropy-induced, training-free approach for quantifying accuracy limits in sequential recommendation, yielding a candidate-size-agnostic estimate. Experiments on controlled synthetic generators and diverse real-world benchmarks show that the estimator tracks oracle-controlled difficulty more faithfully than baselines, remains insensitive to candidate-set size, and achieves high rank consistency with best-achieved offline accuracy across state-of-the-art sequential recommenders (Spearman rho up to 0.914). It also supports user-group diagnostics by stratifying users by novelty preference, long-tail exposure, and activity, revealing systematic predictability differences. Furthermore, predictability can guide training data selection: training sets constructed from high-predictability users yield strong downstream performance under reduced data budgets. Overall, the proposed estimator provides a practical reference for assessing attainable accuracy limits, supporting user-group diagnostics, and informing data-centric decisions in sequential recommendation.

</details>


### [385] [RCLRec: Reverse Curriculum Learning for Modeling Sparse Conversions in Generative Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.28124)
*Yulei Huang,Hao Deng,Haibo Xing,Jinxin Hu,Chuanfei Xu,Zulong Chen,Yu Zhang,Xiaoyi Zeng*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: RCLRec uses reverse curriculum learning to address conversion sparsity in generative recommendation by selecting conversion-related subsequences from user history as intermediate supervision.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conversion objectives in large-scale recommender systems are sparse and difficult to optimize. Existing generative recommendation models with behavior-aware attention still rely on full history attention and lack additional supervision for conversions, leaving conversion sparsity unresolved.

Method: Proposes RCLRec, a reverse curriculum learning-based GR framework. For each conversion target, constructs a short curriculum by selecting a subsequence of conversion-related items from history in reverse. Semantic tokens are fed to decoder as prefix with target conversion tokens under joint generation objective. Includes curriculum quality-aware loss to ensure selected curricula are informative.

Result: Experiments on offline datasets and online A/B test show superior performance, achieving +2.09% advertising revenue and +1.86% orders in online deployment.

Conclusion: RCLRec effectively addresses conversion sparsity in generative recommendation by providing instance-specific intermediate supervision through reverse curriculum learning, focusing the model on critical decision processes and improving conversion prediction.

Abstract: Conversion objectives in large-scale recommender systems are sparse, making them difficult to optimize. Generative recommendation (GR) partially alleviates data sparsity by organizing multi-type behaviors into a unified token sequence with shared representations, but conversion signals remain insufficiently modeled. While recent behavior-aware GR models encode behavior types and employ behavior-aware attention to highlight decision-related intermediate behaviors, they still rely on standard attention over the full history and provide no additional supervision for conversions, leaving conversion sparsity largely unresolved. To address these challenges, we propose RCLRec, a reverse curriculum learning-based GR framework for sparse conversion supervision. For each conversion target, RCLRec constructs a short curriculum by selecting a subsequence of conversion-related items from the history in reverse. Their semantic tokens are fed to the decoder as a prefix, together with the target conversion tokens, under a joint generation objective. This design provides additional instance-specific intermediate supervision, alleviating conversion sparsity and focusing the model on the user's critical decision process. We further introduce a curriculum quality-aware loss to ensure that the selected curricula are informative for conversion prediction. Experiments on offline datasets and an online A/B test show that RCLRec achieves superior performance, with +2.09% advertising revenue and +1.86% orders in online deployment.

</details>


### [386] [With a Little Help From My Friends: Collective Manipulation in Risk-Controlling Recommender Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.28476)
*Giovanni De Toni,Cristian Consonni,Erasmo Purificato,Emilia Gomez,Bruno Lepri*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: Risk-controlling recommender systems using binary user feedback are vulnerable to coordinated adversarial manipulation by small user groups, degrading recommendation quality by up to 20% for non-adversarial users.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To investigate vulnerabilities in risk-controlling recommender systems that use binary user feedback (e.g., "Not Interested") for safety guarantees, particularly their susceptibility to coordinated adversarial manipulation by users exploiting platform affordances.

Method: Empirical analysis using data from a large-scale online video-sharing platform, evaluating simple realistic attack strategies requiring minimal knowledge of the recommendation algorithm, and proposing a mitigation strategy shifting guarantees from group to user level.

Result: A small coordinated group (1% of users) can induce up to 20% degradation in nDCG for non-adversarial users; coordinated attacks harm overall recommendation quality but cannot selectively suppress specific content groups through reporting alone.

Conclusion: Risk-controlling recommender systems are inherently vulnerable to coordinated adversarial behavior due to reliance on aggregate feedback; shifting safety guarantees from group to user level can mitigate these attacks while ensuring personalized safety.

Abstract: Recommendation systems have become central gatekeepers of online information, shaping user behaviour across a wide range of activities. In response, users increasingly organize and coordinate to steer algorithmic outcomes toward diverse goals, such as promoting relevant content or limiting harmful material, relying on platform affordances -- such as likes, reviews, or ratings. While these mechanisms can serve beneficial purposes, they can also be leveraged for adversarial manipulation, particularly in systems where such feedback directly informs safety guarantees. In this paper, we study this vulnerability in recently proposed risk-controlling recommender systems, which use binary user feedback (e.g., "Not Interested") to provably limit exposure to unwanted content via conformal risk control. We empirically demonstrate that their reliance on aggregate feedback signals makes them inherently susceptible to coordinated adversarial user behaviour. Using data from a large-scale online video-sharing platform, we show that a small coordinated group (comprising only 1% of the user population) can induce up to a 20% degradation in nDCG for non-adversarial users by exploiting the affordances provided by risk-controlling recommender systems. We evaluate simple, realistic attack strategies that require little to no knowledge of the underlying recommendation algorithm and find that, while coordinated users can significantly harm overall recommendation quality, they cannot selectively suppress specific content groups through reporting alone. Finally, we propose a mitigation strategy that shifts guarantees from the group level to the user level, showing empirically how it can reduce the impact of adversarial coordinated behaviour while ensuring personalized safety for individuals.

</details>
